To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the overexpression in V-H4 rodent cells of MT-II, a metal-binding protein that regulates the activation of NF-kappaB, is responsible for the hypersensitivity of these rodent cells to DNA cross-linking agent through inhibition of NF-kappa B activation.
overexpression of MTII sensitizes rodent cells to MMC-induced apoptosis by inhibiting the activation of NF-kB.
overexpression of MTII in V-H4 hamsters cells sensitizes these cells to apoptosis induced by DNA cross-linking agent through inhibition of NF-κ-B activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the molecular basis of the MMC hypersensitivity of the V-H4 cell line, which may be useful in designing new strategies to improve cancer therapy with MMC.
the identification of a novel mechanism that contributes to the sensitivity of cells to MMC, which is based on an altered regulation of the apoptotic response.
the identification of genes that are involved in the sensitivity of cells to MMC and with the molecular mechanisms by which they exert their effect.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the overexpression and/or the inappropriate regulation of the MT-II gene may contribute to the hypersensitivity of V-H4 cells to the cytotoxicity of DNA cross-linking drugs.
MT-II overproduction in the V-H4 cell line is a critical factor in the hypersensitivity of these rodent cells to DNA cross-linking damage.

the increased sensitivity to DNA cross-linking agent of the V-H4 cells is associated with the overexpression of metallothioneins and that this is due to the impairment of DNA repair and/or the inhibition of NF-κb activation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MT-II overexpressing cells are more susceptible to apoptosis induced by cross-linking agents through inhibition of NF-κβ activation.
MT-II overproduction in V-H4 hamsters sensitizes cells to MMC-induced apoptosis through inhibition of NF-κ B activation, which may be a novel mechanism of the antitumor activity of MMC.
MT-II overexpressed in V-H4 sensitizes cells to apoptosis induced by cross-linking agents, at least partially, through inhibition of NF-κb activation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the overexpression and the down-regulation of a specific protein, in our case MT-II, could be exploited as a tool to increase the cytotoxicity of DNA cross-linking drugs.
MT-II is a novel target for cancer therapy.
MT-II overexpressing cells are more susceptible to DNA cross-linking agent induced apoptosis.
